title: What is rebasing in Git, what are its advantages, when do you use it, and what are the risks of rewriting history?
shortTitle: Git rebasing — what it is, advantages, when to use, and the risks of rewriting history

s1_definition.profdef: Rebasing in Git takes the commits on your branch and replays them one by one on top of a new base commit, producing new commit objects with new hashes. It is commonly used to update a feature branch onto the latest main so that history becomes linear, and interactively to clean up a messy series of commits before sharing. Its advantage is a clean, linear history; its central risk is that because it rewrites commits, doing it on shared branches breaks everyone else's copy.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine you started drafting a set of ledger corrections at National Bank of India based on last Monday's official ledger. By Friday the official ledger has moved on with other corrections. Rebasing is like carefully re-writing your corrections fresh, as if you had started from Friday's up-to-date ledger instead of Monday's, so your changes slot cleanly on top with no messy "merge" note explaining the two versions diverged. The danger is that if you rewrite entries a colleague has already copied and is building on, their copy no longer matches the official record, and now the books disagree.
s1_definition.oneliner: Rebase replays your commits onto a new base for a clean linear history, but because it creates new commits it must never be done on branches others have already pulled.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Rebasing in Git takes the commits on your branch and replays them one by one on top of a new base commit, producing new commit objects with new hashes. It is commonly used to update a feature branch onto the latest main so that history becomes linear, and interactively to clean up a messy series of commits before sharing. Its advantage is a clean, linear history; its central risk is that because it rewrites commits, doing it on shared branches breaks everyone else's copy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine you started drafting a set of ledger corrections at National Bank of India based on last Monday's official ledger. By Friday the official ledger has moved on with other corrections. Rebasing is like carefully re-writing your corrections fresh, as if you had started from Friday's up-to-date ledger instead of Monday's, so your changes slot cleanly on top with no messy "merge" note explaining the two versions diverged. The danger is that if you rewrite entries a colleague has already copied and is building on, their copy no longer matches the official record, and now the books disagree.

**One line to remember:** Rebase replays your commits onto a new base for a clean linear history, but because it creates new commits it must never be done on branches others have already pulled.

sections.s2_technical:
To understand rebase you first picture how a branch diverges. You branch off main at some commit, and then both your branch and main gain new commits, so the two lines diverge. There are two ways to bring main's new commits into your branch: merge and rebase. Merge creates a new merge commit that joins the two lines, preserving the exact branched history but leaving a fork in the graph. Rebase instead moves the base of your branch: it takes each of your commits, sets them aside, fast-forwards your branch to the tip of main, and then re-applies your commits one at a time on top. The result looks as if you had started your work from the current main all along — a single straight line.

The crucial technical fact is that rebase does not move your original commits; it creates brand-new commit objects with new hashes. A commit's hash is derived from its content plus its parent, so when the parent changes, the hash changes. Your old commits are abandoned and new equivalent ones take their place. This is why rebasing is called rewriting history — the commit identities genuinely change.

The first advantage is a clean, linear history. After rebasing feature branches onto main before merging, git log reads like a straight story with no tangle of merge commits, which makes it far easier to read, to bisect when hunting a bug, and to understand what happened and in what order. Many teams prefer this over a history full of "Merge branch main into feature" commits that add noise.

The second use is interactive rebase, run with git rebase dash i. This lets you reshape your own local commits before sharing: squash several tiny work-in-progress commits into one meaningful commit, reword confusing commit messages, reorder commits, or drop a commit that should not be there. For a bank where every commit should map cleanly to a reviewed change, cleaning up a messy local history into a few logical commits before opening a pull request makes review much easier.

When do you use it. You rebase your own local, unshared feature branch onto the latest main to stay current and to keep history linear, and you use interactive rebase to tidy your local commits before you push and open a pull request. You do NOT rebase commits that other people have already pulled.

That brings us to the risks of rewriting history, which are serious. Because rebase replaces commits with new ones, if you rebase a branch that a teammate has already based work on, their history still points at your old commits, which no longer exist on the remote. When they try to integrate, Git sees two divergent histories, producing confusing conflicts and sometimes duplicated commits. If someone force-pushes a rebased shared branch, they can overwrite commits others pushed, effectively losing work. The golden rule is: never rebase public or shared history. Only rebase commits that live solely on your machine or on a branch nobody else is using. A related risk is force-pushing — after rebasing you must force-push because the remote branch diverged, and a careless force-push without protection can destroy commits. The safe habit is to use force-with-lease, which refuses to overwrite if the remote has changed since you last fetched. A senior-level nuance: many banking teams forbid rebasing shared branches entirely and allow it only on personal feature branches before the first review, precisely because the audit trail must never be silently rewritten.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has an engineer building a statement-generator feature while main keeps advancing, and the engineer also has a messy set of local commits to clean up.

Problem 1 — the feature branch was cut three days ago and main has moved on, so a plain merge would litter history with merge commits and make the eventual review hard to read. This is exactly where rebasing onto main helps — it replays the feature commits on top of the latest main for a clean linear history.

Problem 2 — the engineer has five tiny commits like "wip", "fix typo", and "oops" that would embarrass a reviewer and pollute the audit trail. This is exactly where interactive rebase helps — squash them into one clear, well-described commit before opening the pull request.

Problem 3 — a junior engineer once rebased a branch that a teammate had already pulled and force-pushed it, and the teammate lost a morning's work. This is exactly the risk the team must guard against — never rebase shared history, and only force-push with lease on personal branches.

The mini-project is a git walkthrough showing rebasing a feature branch onto main, an interactive rebase to squash commits, and a demonstration of the danger of rebasing shared history. A small StatementGenerator Java class is the feature being built so the commits map to real code.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# See the graph BEFORE and AFTER a rebase to observe the linearization.
git log --oneline --graph --all

# Run the feature's tests after rebasing to confirm nothing broke.
mvn test

# Recover if a rebase went wrong: reflog shows where HEAD used to be.
git reflog
git reset --hard HEAD@{3}   # jump back to the pre-rebase state
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a feature branch feature/monthly-statement with three commits, cut from main three days ago, while main has gained two new commits since.

Step 1: The engineer runs git fetch to get main's two new commits into the local repository. The branch and main have now clearly diverged — they share a common ancestor but each has unique commits.

Step 2: The engineer runs git rebase origin/main. Git identifies the three feature commits, sets them aside, and moves the branch's starting point forward to the tip of main. So far no feature commit exists on the new base yet.

Step 3: Git replays the first feature commit on top of the new main, creating a brand-new commit with a new hash because its parent changed. It repeats for the second and third commits. The original three commits are now abandoned; three new equivalent commits exist.

Step 4: A conflict appears on the second commit because both the feature and a new main commit touched StatementGenerator. Git pauses, the engineer edits the file to resolve it, runs git add and git rebase continue, and the replay finishes. History is now a clean straight line.

Step 5: Because the branch diverged from its old remote state, the engineer pushes with force-with-lease. The lease check confirms nobody else pushed to the branch meanwhile, so the overwrite is safe, and the remote now shows the linear history.

Step 6: Separately, the engineer runs interactive rebase to squash five messy local commits into one well-described commit before this was ever pushed, which is safe precisely because those commits were never shared.

```
Oct 25, 2026 03:20:02 AM INFO: fetch: main advanced by 2 commits
Oct 25, 2026 03:20:05 AM INFO: rebase: replaying 3 feature commits onto origin/main
Oct 25, 2026 03:20:06 AM WARNING: conflict in StatementGenerator.java (commit 2/3)
Oct 25, 2026 03:21:40 AM INFO: conflict resolved -> rebase --continue
Oct 25, 2026 03:21:42 AM INFO: rebase complete: linear history, 3 NEW commit hashes
Oct 25, 2026 03:22:10 AM INFO: push --force-with-lease OK (remote unchanged since fetch)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  BEFORE rebase (diverged):

        A───B           feature (3 commits: A,B,C... shown A,B here)
       /
  o───o───M1───M2       main advanced (M1, M2)

  git rebase origin/main
    │ set aside A,B
    │ move base to M2
    │ replay A->A'  (new hash, parent=M2)
    │ replay B->B'  (new hash, parent=A') [conflict here -> resolve]
    ▼
  AFTER rebase (linear):

  o───o───M1───M2───A'───B'   feature (NEW commits on top of main)

    │ push --force-with-lease (safe: remote unchanged since fetch)
    ▼
  remote feature = linear history

  SHARED-HISTORY DANGER:
    teammate still has A,B  ──┐
    A,B no longer on remote   ├─► divergent history, conflicts, lost work
    careless --force overwrites┘   (RULE: never rebase shared branches)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Rebase in the Team Workflow (NBI statements) ═══

  ┌──────────────┐          ┌────────────────────┐
  │ Engineer     │  fetch   │  Git Host (remote) │  ← source of shared truth
  │ local repo   │◀────────▶│  main, feature     │
  └──────┬───────┘          └────────────────────┘
         │ rebase onto origin/main (LOCAL, private commits only)
         │ interactive squash (clean up before sharing)
         ▼
  ┌────────────────────┐
  │ clean linear branch │
  └─────────┬──────────┘
            │ push --force-with-lease (personal branch only)
            ▼
  ┌────────────────────┐  PR  ┌────────────────────┐
  │ Git Host feature    │─────▶│ CI: build + tests   │  ← Application Layer
  └────────────────────┘      └─────────┬──────────┘
                                        │ merge (clean history)
                                        ▼
                               ┌────────────────────┐
                               │ main (linear, audit │  ← readable, bisectable
                               │ trail preserved)    │
                               └────────────────────┘

  Guardrail: branch protection forbids force-push to main/shared branches
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — How Rebase Rewrites Commits ═══

  ┌─ Rebase Principles ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  New identity   : new parent -> new hash (history rewritten)  │
  │  Linear history : replay commits on top of new base          │
  │  Local only     : rebase unshared branches, NEVER shared      │
  │  Safe push      : --force-with-lease, never raw --force        │
  │  Recovery       : git reflog restores pre-rebase state        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Commit Object Identity ─────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ commit B                 │
  │  tree   : <content>      │
  │  parent : A              │───► hash = f(content, parent)
  │  message: ...            │
  └──────────────────────────┘
        rebase changes parent A -> A'
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ commit B' (NEW)          │  parent=A'  => DIFFERENT hash
  └──────────────────────────┘   (old B abandoned)

  ── State Diagram: Rebase Operation ────────────────────────

  [branch diverged] ──rebase start──→ [replaying commits]
        │                                   │ conflict
        │                                   ▼
        │                            [paused: resolve]
        │                                   │ add + --continue
        │                                   ▼
        │                            [replaying commits]
        │                                   │ all applied
        │                                   ▼
        │                            [linear history]
        └── --abort ──→ [restored to pre-rebase state]

  ── Call Chain (rebase + cleanup) ──────────────────────────

  1. git fetch origin                (get new main commits)
  2. git rebase origin/main          (replay my commits)
  3.   → resolve conflicts, --continue
  4. git rebase -i HEAD~5            (squash messy locals)
  5. git push --force-with-lease     (safe overwrite, personal branch)
  6. (if wrong) git reflog + reset   (recover)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Rebasing takes the commits on my branch and replays them one at a time on top of a new base commit — usually the latest main. The crucial technical point is that it does not move my original commits; it creates brand-new commit objects with new hashes, because a commit's hash depends on its content and its parent, and rebase changes the parent. That is exactly why rebasing is called rewriting history — the commit identities genuinely change.

The main advantage is a clean, linear history. When I rebase a feature branch onto main before merging, the log reads like a straight story with no tangle of merge commits, which makes it far easier to read, to bisect when hunting a bug, and to understand what happened in what order. The second use is interactive rebase, where I reshape my own local commits before sharing — squashing several messy work-in-progress commits into one meaningful commit, rewording messages, or dropping a bad commit. In a bank, where every commit should map cleanly to a reviewed change, that tidy-up makes review and the audit trail much better.

So when do I use it: I rebase my own local, unshared feature branch onto the latest main to stay current and linear, and I use interactive rebase to clean up my local commits before I push and open a pull request. The risks are where I am most careful. Because rebase replaces commits with new ones, if I rebase a branch a teammate has already pulled and built on, their history points at commits that no longer exist on the remote, which produces confusing divergent conflicts and, with a careless force-push, can overwrite and lose their work.

My golden rule is never rebase public or shared history — only rebase commits that live solely on my machine or on a personal branch nobody else is using. When I do need to push a rebased personal branch, I use force-with-lease rather than a raw force push, because lease refuses to overwrite if the remote changed since my last fetch. And if a rebase ever goes wrong, git reflog lets me find where HEAD used to be and reset back. At National Bank of India many teams allow rebasing only on personal feature branches before the first review and forbid it on shared branches entirely, precisely because the audit trail must never be silently rewritten.
